questions.q: Why does the lesson say training the same model architecture twice can silently produce two different results?
options: Model training is always fully deterministic, so this never actually happens in practice
Only GPU training is non-deterministic; CPU training always reproduces exactly
A different random seed, an unrecorded hyperparameter tweak, or a dependency version bump can all change the outcome without anyone writing it down
It only happens if the training script is rewritten from scratch each time
questions.explain: Without systematic logging, small unrecorded differences — seeds, hyperparameters, dependency versions — can silently change a training run's outcome, making 'reproduce this result' a guessing game.

questions.q: What does an experiment tracking tool like MLflow log for a training run?
options: Only the final validation accuracy number, nothing else
The hyperparameters used, the resulting metrics, the code version, and the resulting model artifact
The GPU driver version installed on the training cluster, exclusively
The Kubernetes namespace the training job happened to run in
questions.explain: Experiment tracking logs hyperparameters, metrics, code version (commit hash), and the resulting artifact for every run, making results reproducible and comparable later.

questions.q: How does a model registry differ from experiment tracking, according to this lesson?
options: A registry is just another name for the same tracking server with no functional difference
A registry only works with GPU-trained models, never CPU-trained ones
A registry replaces the need to log any training metrics at all
A registry is a versioned catalog of models worth keeping, each with a promotion stage, while tracking logs every training attempt regardless of whether it's kept
questions.explain: Experiment tracking logs every run; a model registry sits on top of that and holds only the versioned models worth keeping, each with an explicit stage like Staging or Production.

questions.q: What does promoting a model from Staging to Production in a registry actually represent?
options: A deliberate, logged, auditable action that makes which version is actually serving traffic an explicit, answerable claim
An automatic process that happens the instant a training run finishes, with no evaluation
A renaming of the model file with no change in behavior or deployment
A one-way action that can never be reversed once performed
questions.explain: A registry makes promotion a deliberate, auditable action rather than an unrecorded file copy — and rollback means pointing the Production alias back at a previous version.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call experiment tracking and model registries 'the foundation everything else in this chapter builds on'?
options: Because GPU provisioning from earlier chapters depends directly on the registry's API
Because monitoring only works if experiment tracking is disabled
Because CI/CD for models and monitoring both need to know which registered version is currently in production to compare against or alert on
Because CI/CD pipelines cannot run at all without a registry, even for application code unrelated to models
questions.explain: CI/CD gates (lesson 19) need the registry to know the current production version to compare a new candidate against, and monitoring (lesson 20) needs to know which version is actually deployed.
